definition: Congenital visual impairment is reduced vision that is present from birth. In the supplied psychology context, it is described as an early-life visual condition associated in children with altered visual integration and stronger Müller-Lyer illusion effects than in visually normal peers.

reasons: The packet does not directly support the gloss “reduced vision that is present from birth”; it refers to children with congenital visual impairment but does not define the term in those words.

“Altered visual integration” is only indirectly suggested by the paper’s discussion that early-life abnormal visual experiences may adversely affect integration, not stated as a direct description of the condition.

The definition states that the condition is “reduced vision that is present from birth,” but the supplied packet does not explicitly define congenital visual impairment as reduced vision present from birth.

Although the packet discusses that “abnormal visual experiences during early-life may adversely affect integration in congenitally visually impaired children,” it does not directly support the wording “altered visual integration” as stated in the definition.

The packet supports that children aged 4–17 with congenital visual impairment show “heightened intensity of Müller-Lyer illusion compared to visually normal counterparts,” but the overall definition includes additional elements (especially the birth/present-from-birth phrasing) that are not supported.
